tracks.title: Know the panel

lessons.title: Read the panel and follow the soft keys
lessons.summary: Start with a healthy fictional panel, open Info and practise leaving a menu without changing a system condition.
prerequisites: The practice panel is in its normal scenario.
The outer-door controls are available in the fictional training panel.

steps.title: Check the starting condition
steps.explanation: Read the healthy status and identify the green Power lamp. A quiet buzzer alone would not prove that the system is healthy.
steps.expected: No fire, fault, disablement or test condition is present.
steps.commonMistake: Skipping the display and deciding that quiet means healthy.

steps.title: Open the menus
steps.explanation: Menu On/Off reveals the four current function-key choices. The condition being reported remains present underneath the menu.
steps.expected: The first row offers Control, Set Up, Info and Test/Eng.
steps.commonMistake: Expecting Menu On/Off to acknowledge or clear an event.

steps.title: Choose Info
steps.explanation: F3 currently selects Info because that label is above it. Its job will change on other menu pages.
steps.expected: Active and Historic viewing choices appear.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current soft-key label before choosing the next function.

steps.title: Use the next group of choices
steps.explanation: The <etc> label means more choices in this menu. It is not a universal back or confirm key.
steps.expected: The next Info group includes Label.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current soft-key label before choosing the next function.

steps.title: Abort the menu
steps.explanation: One press of Menu On/Off aborts the current menu operation and returns to the status display.
steps.expected: The menu is closed and the underlying healthy condition is unchanged.
steps.commonMistake: Expecting the same key to reset or acknowledge a condition.

lessons.restoreInstruction: No protection state was changed. You can reopen Menu On/Off to continue practising.

lessons.title: Run the display and indicator test
lessons.summary: Use the documented two-menu route and understand what the short test proves.
prerequisites: Start from the normal fictional scenario.
Browser sound may be muted; the visual training result remains available.

steps.title: Open the menus
steps.explanation: Menu On/Off reveals the four current function-key choices. The condition being reported remains present underneath the menu.
steps.expected: The first row offers Control, Set Up, Info and Test/Eng.
steps.commonMistake: Expecting Menu On/Off to acknowledge or clear an event.

steps.title: Choose Test/Eng
steps.explanation: The first Test/Eng group contains the operator display test. Selecting it does not grant engineering access.
steps.expected: Disp Test is available above F1.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current soft-key label before choosing the next function.

steps.title: Start Disp Test
steps.explanation: Check the display, indicators and internal buzzer simulation. The operator manual describes a test lasting about four seconds.
steps.expected: The display-test sequence starts; indicators illuminate and two test tones are represented.
steps.commonMistake: Assuming this indication test has exercised the detection loops or every building sounder.

steps.title: Understand the result
steps.explanation: Observe the display returning to its status presentation. This exercise checks the panel indications, not the entire detection and alarm installation.
steps.expected: Wait for the approximately four-second sequence to finish and the healthy state to return.
steps.commonMistake: Interpreting a display test as evidence that external signalling or protection equipment worked.

lessons.restoreInstruction: The test returns to the panel display. It does not intentionally leave any zone or device disabled.

lessons.title: Read a fire and acknowledge the buzzer
lessons.summary: Practise the smallest sound-control action and verify what it leaves unchanged.
prerequisites: The lesson generates a fictional Reception sensor fire.
Real emergency actions follow the site response procedure; this exercise only changes the simulation.

steps.title: Read the fire location
steps.explanation: This fictional fire is at the Reception optical sensor, L1D1 in Z1. Read the first-fire information and the red indications before touching a sound control.
steps.expected: A fire is latched, the buzzer is sounding and the system alarms are active.
steps.commonMistake: Silencing before reading where the event occurred.

steps.title: Cancel the panel buzzer
steps.explanation: This button acknowledges the local audible indication. It does not silence the system alarm sounders or clear the fire.
steps.expected: The internal buzzer stops, while the fire and system alarms remain active.
steps.commonMistake: Pressing Silence Alarms because you intend to quiet only the panel buzzer.

steps.title: Check what stayed active
steps.explanation: The red fire indication and building-alarm state remain. The quiet panel buzzer has not made this a normal condition.
steps.expected: Fire remains active and the system alarms are still sounding.
steps.commonMistake: Assuming acknowledgement means the emergency is over.

lessons.restoreInstruction: This lesson intentionally leaves the fictional fire and alarm sounders active. The restore-and-reset lesson teaches their separate recovery.

lessons.title: Read the first and later fires
lessons.summary: Browse multiple fictional events while keeping the first fire in view.
prerequisites: The multiple-fires scenario supplies three fictional sensor events.
No silence or reset is required to browse them.

steps.title: Find the first fire
steps.explanation: The first event remains at the top. Subsequent events occupy the lower event area; the fixture includes enough later events to practise scrolling.
steps.expected: The display has a pinned first fire and a separate later-fire position.
steps.commonMistake: Assuming the display only contains one fire.

steps.title: Move to the next later fire
steps.explanation: Use the physical Next event control. It browses the later fire entries without acknowledging or clearing them.
steps.expected: The lower fire detail changes; the first-fire detail stays pinned.
steps.commonMistake: Confusing the physical fire-scroll control with a menu F3 option on another screen.

steps.title: Return to the previous later fire
steps.explanation: Use Previous to compare the earlier later-fire entry with the one just seen.
steps.expected: The lower event changes back and the first fire remains at the top.
steps.commonMistake: Expecting browsing to remove the later event.

steps.title: Remember what the lamps can prove
steps.explanation: Zonal lamps identify affected zones. The source makes flashing of the first zone a commissioned option, so do not depend on that convention without site verification.
steps.expected: All fictional fires remain active after browsing.
steps.commonMistake: Treating a possible flashing-zone convention as universal.

lessons.restoreInstruction: Browsing changes no fire input. Load the normal scenario or complete the recovery workflow when finished.

lessons.title: Silence and sound the system alarms
lessons.summary: Separate panel-buzzer acknowledgement from the two physical system-alarm controls.
prerequisites: The fire is fictional.
The lesson includes an explicit agreed-test context before silence and re-sound.

steps.title: Acknowledge the local buzzer
steps.explanation: First quiet the local panel indication so the two sound systems are easy to distinguish.
steps.expected: The buzzer stops but system sounders remain active.
steps.commonMistake: Calling all audible outputs the buzzer.

steps.title: Confirm the exercise condition
steps.explanation: In this fictional exercise the test leader now authorises alarm silence. The operator manual places silence after the emergency or agreed test has ended.
steps.expected: You are deliberately choosing the building-alarm control, not clearing the input.
steps.commonMistake: Treating silence as the first response to an unknown real fire.

steps.title: Silence the system alarms
steps.explanation: Silence Alarms stops system sounders. The latched fire remains for investigation and later reset.
steps.expected: System sounders stop and the fire remains displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Expecting Silence Alarms to clear the fire indication.

steps.title: Sound the alarms again
steps.explanation: Sound Alarms is the direct physical control for an emergency or agreed alarm exercise. Here it re-sounds the fictional system.
steps.expected: System sounders are active again; the fire has not been reset.
steps.commonMistake: Pressing Reset to try to make the alarms sound again.

lessons.restoreInstruction: The sounders are deliberately left active at the end. Practise restoring the input, silencing and resetting in the next exercise.

lessons.title: Restore the input, then reset the fire
lessons.summary: Learn the difference between a normal detector input and a cleared, latched panel event.
prerequisites: The exercise uses L1D1 only.
The trainer action represents investigation being complete; it does not teach a real repair.

steps.title: Cancel the buzzer
steps.explanation: Acknowledge the internal buzzer without assuming that the detector has returned to normal.
steps.expected: The buzzer is quiet; the fictional fire remains.
steps.commonMistake: Confusing acknowledgement with restored detection.

steps.title: Silence after the fictional test ends
steps.explanation: The agreed fictional test is over. Silence the system alarms before the recovery check.
steps.expected: Sounders are silent and the fire is still latched.
steps.commonMistake: Assuming silence is the same as reset.

steps.title: Restore the simulated detector input
steps.explanation: This is a trainer control, not a panel key. It represents the initiating condition having cleared after investigation.
steps.expected: L1D1 is normal, but the panel fire remains latched until Reset.
steps.commonMistake: Trying to clear an active detector condition by repeatedly pressing Reset.

steps.title: Reset the panel indication
steps.explanation: The fictional input is now normal. Reset clears the remaining latched fire state.
steps.expected: The fire clears and the panel returns to its normal condition.
steps.commonMistake: Resetting while a call point remains operated or a detector input is still active.

steps.title: Check the final indications
steps.explanation: Confirm the healthy display and green Power indication; look for any separate fault, disablement or test indication before concluding the exercise.
steps.expected: No fictional event or disablement remains.
steps.commonMistake: Checking only that the red Fire lamp has gone out.

lessons.restoreInstruction: The fictional panel is healthy at completion. Record-keeping is a site task separate from pressing Reset.

lessons.title: Acknowledge and investigate a fault
lessons.summary: Read an active device fault, separate acknowledgement from repair and verify its fictional clearance.

The trainer clear-fault button represents external correction, not panel repair.

steps.title: Read the device fault
steps.explanation: The fictional fault concerns L1D3, the Ground office sensor. The display identifies the fault; the amber indication is not a red fire indication.
steps.expected: A device fault is active and the panel buzzer is sounding.
steps.commonMistake: Treating the amber fault as a confirmed fire or ignoring its address.

steps.title: Cancel the fault buzzer
steps.explanation: Stop the local audible indication. The responsible servicing engineer still needs the fault details on a real installation.
steps.expected: The buzzer stops but the fault stays active.
steps.commonMistake: Assuming the fault has been repaired because the panel is quiet.

steps.title: Choose Active

steps.expected: The Active event query is ready.

steps.title: Display active events

lessons.restoreInstruction: No fault remains in this simulation. Real fault details and repair arrangements belong in the site record.

helpArticles.title: Which GENT panel am I practising?
helpArticles.summary: This module follows the full-size Vigilon 4/6-loop panel with the 2015 2 km-loop documentation.
helpArticles.body:
The recognisable face, four function keys and QWERTY keyboard belong to the selected full-size Vigilon generation. Compact, Nano, Plus, Network Node and BS variants can have different controls or menu behaviour.

FINDR uses a small invented building on loops 1 and 2. Its addresses, labels, events and practice PIN are training data. Site documents determine the corresponding information on a real installation. The source register records the inconsistent edition markings in the operator PDF.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming every panel carrying the GENT or Vigilon name has this exact menu.

helpArticles.title: What should a healthy panel show?
helpArticles.summary: With no fire, fault, disablement or test condition, check the healthy message and green Power indication.
helpArticles.body:
The operator manual describes the normal display as Panel healthy with only the green Power indicator lit. Read the message as well as the lamps. A silenced buzzer is not evidence that the system is healthy.

In FINDR the final recovery exercise leaves every fictional detector normal, clears its fault, re-enables its zone and checks the remaining indicators. Opening a menu does not itself restore a condition.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating quiet sounders or a quiet panel buzzer as an all-clear.

helpArticles.title: Read the indicators together
helpArticles.summary: Colour identifies the type of condition; the display identifies what caused it.
helpArticles.body:
Fire is the red fire indication. Fault, Power Fault, System Fault, Disablement and Test identify different conditions and are not interchangeable. The green Power lamp says that a supply is present.

The Sounder lamp is interpreted with Fault or Disablement: the source describes flashing for a sounder fault and steady for sounder disablement. A FARE Fault/Dis lamp has its own combined meaning. Do not infer that a specific output has failed from a single isolated lamp.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Reading the amber Sounder lamp as a simple indication that sounders are currently making noise.

helpArticles.title: Read the event before pressing a control
helpArticles.summary: Use the event type, zone, location label, device and loop together.
helpArticles.body:
The selected panel has an eight-line, forty-character display. A location label helps a person find the affected area, while the zone, device and loop distinguish the point being reported. A device number alone is incomplete because another loop can contain the same number.

For this training building, L1D1 is the Reception optical sensor; L1D2 is the Main entrance manual call point. Z2 is the Ground floor offices zone. These labels are examples, not a numbering standard for other premises.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Entering a zone number in a device field, or using an address without checking its loop.

helpArticles.title: How F1, F2, F3 and F4 work
helpArticles.summary: A function key selects the current label directly above it.
helpArticles.body:
Menu On/Off shows the first menu. F1 through F4 change purpose as the displayed labels change. Read the label before each press; a remembered F2 is not a universal Enter command. The keyboard Enter key is also distinct from a displayed Enter option assigned to a function key.

The Params option explains the kind of entry a field accepts. Menu On/Off aborts the current operation. Where present, Quit leaves the function. The documented panel removes menu prompts after five minutes without a key press.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Pressing the physical Enter key where the current menu explicitly requires F2 Enter.

helpArticles.title: Cancel Buzzer, Silence Alarms and Reset do different jobs
helpArticles.summary: Learn which sound or condition each physical button changes.
helpArticles.body:
Cancel Buzzer stops the internal panel buzzer. It does not silence the alarm sounders around the building. Silence Alarms stops those system alarms when the emergency or agreed test has ended. Sound Alarms starts system alarms for an emergency or agreed exercise.

Reset is a separate action used after the initiating condition has been restored. A detector still responding to smoke or heat, or an unrestored manual call point, can cause a fire indication to return. Re-enabling a disabled device requires its enable menu; Reset is not that operation.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using Reset as a shortcut for silencing, repairing a fault or re-enabling a device.

helpArticles.title: First fire and subsequent fires
helpArticles.summary: The first fire remains at the top while you browse the later events.
helpArticles.body:
Use Previous and Next to inspect additional fires. The manual keeps the first fire at the top of the display and places subsequent fires below it. Each is also recorded in the historic log.

Zonal indications identify affected zones. Whether the first zone flashes is a commissioned option; a tutorial must not treat that flashing convention as guaranteed on every installation.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that the lower event has replaced the first fire or that browsing acknowledges it.

helpArticles.title: Why a fire may return after Reset
helpArticles.summary: The cause needs to be normal before the latched indication can stay cleared.
helpArticles.body:
The operator procedure calls for residual smoke or heat to clear and a manual call point to be restored before Reset. A new fire indication immediately afterwards calls for investigation of the indicated point. Following fire damage, the source calls for the servicing organisation to check the system.

The trainer separates the detector input from the latched panel event. Setting the fictional input to normal does not itself press Reset; pressing Reset while an input remains active does not make that input healthy.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Repeating Reset without checking the initiating point.

helpArticles.title: What does Verify mean?
helpArticles.summary: Verify depends on commissioning and the site response procedure.
helpArticles.body:
When configured, Verify extends the period available to investigate before delayed sounders operate. The delayed outputs still operate after that period expires. It is not a general-purpose acknowledgement or a way to prove that an alarm is false.

FINDR does not invent a universal delay duration or a site response policy. This control is explained as configuration-dependent rather than offered as a generic fastest route for an alarm.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Pressing Verify on an unfamiliar installation simply to make an alarm quieter.

helpArticles.title: Why U1–U4 cannot have universal tutorials
helpArticles.summary: Their tasks are assigned during commissioning.
helpArticles.body:
The four U buttons may be assigned to specific tasks such as a temporary device disablement or a plant action. The operator manual says their functions should be written on a label inside the outer door.

A U1 on one site can do something different from U1 on another site. The selected training model therefore identifies these as site-defined controls instead of silently borrowing an invented assignment.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming a U button is a standard acknowledgement, silence or disable command.

helpArticles.title: Why the menu says Sensing and then Device
helpArticles.summary: Sensing selects the operation; Device and Loop identify its target.
helpArticles.body:
The verified operator route is Control, UserCode, Enable or Disable, then Sensing. The resulting entry asks for Device and then Loop. Those changing words are intentional in this source edition.

Enter the device address and loop from the site record. In the exercise, device 1 on loop 1 is the Reception sensor. Changing device 1 on loop 2 would affect a different fictional sensor.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Looking for a Device option at the first enable/disable menu because that word appears later.

helpArticles.title: Device, zone and sector are different targets
helpArticles.summary: Choose the scope before committing an operation.
helpArticles.body:
A device is an addressed point. A zone is a subdivision of the premises used for fire detection. A sector concerns a configured collection of alarm outputs; it is not simply another name for a detection zone.

The manual warns that an interface output assigned to a sector may require a sector operation, which also affects the other devices in that sector. FINDR teaches point and zone operations with defined fictional targets, and leaves site-specific output relationships clearly outside those drills.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Disabling an entire zone or output sector when only one sensing point was intended.

helpArticles.title: What a disablement tells you
helpArticles.summary: Part of the configured system has intentionally been taken out of operation.
helpArticles.body:
A disablement may be manual or may be scheduled by the installation configuration. The Disable count reports current disablements, and the historic log records their occurrence. Read the displayed target and reason; the condition is not automatically a hardware fault.

Investigate why the part was disabled and restore it when appropriate. A Reset command does not substitute for the matching Enable operation. After restoring it, check the active event list and remaining indicators.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming a disablement will disappear just because the panel has been reset.

helpArticles.title: Manual call points need separate care
helpArticles.summary: The selected operator manual permits only individual MCP disablement and discourages doing it.
helpArticles.body:
The Sensing instructions state that an MCP can only be disabled individually, not as part of a range. They explicitly discourage MCP disablement. A sensing-device demonstration in FINDR therefore uses an optical sensor.

The 2015 operator text does not settle every interaction between zone disablement and MCP response. The zone exercise deliberately uses Z2, a fictional zone without an MCP, rather than teaching an unsupported exception as a universal rule.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that a range or zone operation has the same effect on every type of input.

helpArticles.title: Active events versus historic events
helpArticles.summary: Active is what remains now; Historic is what was recorded.
helpArticles.body:
Active shows fire, fault and disablement conditions that are still present. Historic is the record of past events and may include conditions that have already cleared. A cleared event can therefore remain in history without being an active fault.

Use Active during a recovery check and Historic when reconstructing what happened. When looking through Active, the verified function keys are F2 Previous and F3 Next, with F4 Quit to finish.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Seeing an old fault in history and assuming that it is still active.

helpArticles.title: Historic event 1 is the newest
helpArticles.summary: The documented panel log holds up to 255 entries.
helpArticles.body:
The operator manual numbers the most recent historic entry as 1. Enter an event number in the 1–255 range, then select the displayed Enter option. History is stored in order of events, not by zone or device number.

The trainer uses a short fictional log. Some actions add new entries, so the item that was number 1 can move when another event occurs. Read its time and message before drawing a sequence of events from it.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Entering a device number in the Historic event-number field.

helpArticles.title: Investigating a fault indication
helpArticles.summary: Acknowledge the internal buzzer, identify the event and record it.
helpArticles.body:
A system fault condition can be raised by a supply failure, lost device or another monitored failure. The display identifies the event; the number beside Fault represents the number of current faults. Cancel Buzzer stops the local sound without correcting the cause.

Record the information and arrange the responsible servicing engineer to rectify the actual installation. The training control that removes a fictional fault is a scenario action, not a panel repair function.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating acknowledgement as a repair or pressing Reset until an underlying fault disappears.

helpArticles.title: Power Fault and System Fault
helpArticles.summary: These indicate different classes of failure.
helpArticles.body:
Power Fault is associated with a mains or battery supply failure. The fault table distinguishes mains failure, a discharged battery and a disconnected battery. Read the full message instead of inferring the cause from the lamp alone.

System Fault concerns the system processor. The operator description warns that fire detection may be affected. These are indications to report to the responsible engineer; the emulator does not teach an unverified repair shortcut.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that a green Power lamp rules out a supply fault elsewhere.

helpArticles.title: What a lost-device message means
helpArticles.summary: The panel is not communicating with the addressed device over the loop.
helpArticles.body:
The manual uses Lost Device for a device that is not communicating with the control panel through its loop. A sounder device may add a Sounder indication. The same symptom does not prove a single physical cause.

Capture the device, loop and location label for the service record. The FINDR removed-device scenario is a fictional example of a device fault; its training description does not assert that every real panel firmware uses the same text.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that a communication fault is a fire alarm or that the device itself must be defective.

helpArticles.title: FARE and FPE are not the building sounders
helpArticles.summary: Routing and protection equipment have their own functions and indications.
helpArticles.body:
FARE means Fire Alarm Routing Equipment and relates to signalling to an alarm receiving centre. FPE means Fire Protection Equipment. Their controls should not be confused with Cancel Buzzer or the system alarm controls.

The operator manual gives separate FARE and FPE operations and warns against using a sector disablement to disable FARE. Some printed menu positions differ between the sources. FINDR explains their purpose and source limits without claiming an unverified control route.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using a sector operation as an assumed substitute for the documented FARE operation.

helpArticles.title: Vigilon walk test: start GENT Zone Test and follow the cycle
helpArticles.summary: The documented engineering route has two Test selections and a default five-second alarm cycle.
helpArticles.body:
FINDR calls this a walk test; the GENT menu calls it Zone Test. The selected profile is the classic full-size EN Vigilon documented in 4188-856 issue 7, July 2015. The complete page-105 map is used for the controls; page 81 gives the cycle and finishing instructions. A separate Vigilon Plus training slide corroborates the repeated Test selection and direct zone entry, without extending the trainer’s claim to every Plus or later firmware.

In the fictional fixture the route is Menu On/Off → F4 Test/Eng → F4 UserCode → engineering practice PIN 3917 → keyboard Enter → F4 <etc> → F2 Test → F4 Test → F2 On → zone 2 → F2 Enter. There is no extra Zone button after On. The engineering PIN is invented for FINDR; customer practice PIN 2468 is a different access level.

With the default automatic silence/reset mode, a fire input in the tested zone sounds the simulated alarms for about five seconds, then the alarms silence and the test fire resets. Zone Test remains selected and the Test indication stays on. Other zones continue normal operation. This exercise uses L1D3 in Z2; NoReset, NoSilence, ranges and multiple-zone test policies are outside the lesson.

The full guided lesson pauses training time and offers an explicit Advance 5 seconds action, so the learner can inspect both states. Free practice advances the five-second cycle automatically. These are FINDR controls and timing policies, not additional GENT panel keys.

The manual also describes inhibited delay-block, network, auxiliary-relay and clean-contact operation during test. The fixture does not represent or certify the external equipment or cause-and-effect of an installed system.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Skipping one Test selection, pressing an invented Zone key, or mistaking the automatic reset for Test Off.

helpArticles.title: End a Vigilon walk test: switch GENT Zone Test Off
helpArticles.summary: Restore the input, commit the Off route and check the Test indication has gone out.
helpArticles.body:
The five-second automatic silence/reset ends one test alarm cycle. It does not remove the selected zone from Test, and closing the menu does not switch Test Off.

Restore the simulated L1D3 input before finishing. Repeat Menu On/Off → F4 Test/Eng → F4 UserCode → fictional engineering PIN 3917 → keyboard Enter → F4 <etc> → F2 Test → F4 Test. Choose F1 Off, type zone 2 directly and press F2 Enter. No additional Zone selection is required. Close the menu afterwards and inspect the status.

A complete restoration requires the Test indication to go out, the input to remain normal and no remaining fire, fault, disablement or other selected test zone. The end-test lesson starts from the ready-to-finish Zone Test scenario; the full walk-test lesson also includes activation and the five-second cycle.

Restoring an input and completing the site’s checks are distinct from the menu operation. FINDR only changes a fictional fixture. It does not clear or verify any real external output, monitoring arrangement or commissioned cause-and-effect.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Finishing after silence, automatic reset or menu closure while Test is still selected.

helpArticles.title: Weekly test and zone test are different procedures
helpArticles.summary: The operator guide describes a call-point exercise followed by manual acknowledgement, silence and reset.
helpArticles.body:
The selected operator manual describes notifying the alarm receiving centre of the test, operating a manual call point with its test key, checking the sounders and indication, restoring the call point, cancelling the buzzer, silencing the alarms and resetting the panel. It then calls for a log-book entry.

That operator exercise is not the same as the engineering zone-test mode with its automatic five-second cycle. Follow the site test plan and the instructions for the actual call-point model. FINDR uses a simulated input instead of pretending its on-screen button is a real call-point test key.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Mixing the normal operator test sequence with the automatic zone-test mode.

helpArticles.title: What the display test checks
helpArticles.summary: It exercises the panel display, indicators and internal buzzer.
helpArticles.body:
Use Menu On/Off, F4 Test/Eng and F1 Disp Test. The operator guide describes a cleared display, illuminated indicators, two buzzer tones and a return to the status message. The stated duration is about four seconds.

This is a panel indication check. It is not evidence that each detector, interface, sounder circuit or signalling path has been tested. In FINDR the lamps and display are a visual simulation; browser audio settings can affect the training sound.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating a successful display test as a test of the whole fire detection system.

helpArticles.title: Door access and UserCode
helpArticles.summary: Access to the physical controls and authentication for menu operations are separate.
helpArticles.body:
The panel drawing distinguishes controls available with the outer door closed from the controls behind it. Many Control, Set Up and Test/Eng operations also require the site password, called PIN, Usercode or access code in the manuals.

FINDR starts with the fictional practice door open and uses 2468 only as its invented practice PIN. It is not a GENT default and is not offered as a code for a real site. Engineering access is distinct from this customer training access.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that an unlocked outer door automatically authorises every protected menu.

helpArticles.title: Labels and non-volatile memory
helpArticles.summary: Read labels carefully; changes to stored configuration need the documented Save operation.
helpArticles.body:
A label identifies a device, zone, input/output line or local panel. The manual provides separate view and modify routes, so opening a label for display does not edit it. Device and zone labels can contain up to 32 characters; MCP labels have a shorter 28-character limit.

The operator guide requires label and password changes to be saved to panel memory, and says Save is available with an access-level-2 PIN and only when there are no disablements. Treat an on-screen change and a backed-up change as different states.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Thinking that viewing a label edits it, or that a configuration change is permanently stored before Save.

helpArticles.title: Why the clock matters
helpArticles.summary: The timestamp affects both event records and time-related configuration.
helpArticles.body:
The clock menu edits hour, minute, date, month and year in that order. F1 advances to the next field; F2 decreases and F3 increases its value; F4 enters the change. The manual then instructs the operator to save the clock settings.

An incorrect clock can give misleading event times and affect time-related sensor configuration. Automatic daylight-saving adjustment is a commissioned option. The training clock is fictional and does not change your device clock.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using F1 Next to increase a number, or assuming daylight-saving behaviour is identical on every site.

helpArticles.title: Why Info sometimes shows Display and Print
helpArticles.summary: The initial Info choices depend on whether a printer is fitted and switched on.
helpArticles.body:
The operator procedures tell the user to skip the Display/Print choice when a printer is absent or switched off. This training fixture uses that condition, so Info leads directly to its viewing choices.

If a real panel shows Display and Print first, choose Display to follow the equivalent on-screen route. Printer paper-feed and character-test functions concern the fitted printer; they are not extra navigation steps for a printerless installation.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming that one extra Display prompt means the user is on the wrong panel.

glossary.definition: A fire, fault or disablement that remains present, rather than just an entry in history.
The panel record of events; this source describes up to 255 entries with entry 1 the newest.
The enable/disable menu choice used to target a sensing device by Device and Loop.
An addressed loop point, such as a sensor, manual call point or interface.
The loop connection identifying which circuit contains a device; the full-size panel uses numbered loop-card positions.
A subdivision of the premises used for fire detection and location reporting.
Manual call point: a device by which a person can raise a fire alarm.
Fire Alarm Routing Equipment, associated with signalling to an alarm receiving centre.
Fire Protection Equipment, controlled through its configured interfaces.
An input or output line of an interface; identify its line, device and loop separately.
A manual or automatic removal of part of the system from operation that must be investigated and restored when appropriate.
Non-volatile memory: the panel memory used to retain the changes covered by the Save procedure.
The site access password for protected operations; FINDR uses an explicitly fictional practice value.
One of F1–F4, selecting the currently displayed label directly above that key.
Open circuit / short circuit, abbreviations used in monitored wiring fault messages.
A unit providing central indications in a Vigilon network; not all loop-panel operations apply to it.

sourceGaps.title: Conflicting edition markings in the operator PDF
sourceGaps.detail: The preface calls this the second issue, while the final-page footer identifies issue 4 with a July 2015 date. The release identifies the document number and date rather than silently choosing one issue.
sourceGaps.impact: Citations use 4188-1025, July 2015 and printed page numbers.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: An unambiguous manufacturer-controlled revision record for this PDF.

sourceGaps.title: Two-loop entries in a four/six-loop operator document
sourceGaps.detail: Several worked operator procedures print loop 1–2 while the document also identifies four-loop and six-loop hardware. This is not used to redefine the product capacity.
sourceGaps.impact: All interactive lessons use existing fictional points on loops 1 and 2; broad loop-range claims are withheld.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: Verified operator-screen capture for the target firmware on loops 3–6.

sourceGaps.title: Zone-test route pinned to the complete menu map
sourceGaps.detail: Commissioning page 81 abbreviates the route and places Zone in prose before On/Off. The full page-105 map contains two Test selections and shows the Zone entry directly after On/Off. Manufacturer-origin Vigilon Plus training page 103 independently corroborates Test → Test → On/Off → zone number/range → Enter. The interactive drill follows that complete mapped order; it does not add a guessed Zone key.
sourceGaps.impact: Two lessons now teach the single-zone On/Off route and default automatic silence/reset cycle on the selected classic EN fixture. The Plus slide is corroboration only; NoReset/NoSilence, ranges, other models and exact physical firmware parity are not claimed.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A physical menu recording from the selected classic EN firmware would strengthen the remaining hardware-parity check. The archive filename is not a verified issue date for the Plus presentation.

sourceGaps.title: The selected edition does not resolve every zone/MCP interaction
sourceGaps.detail: The 2015 Sensing procedure limits MCP disablement to an individual point and discourages it. Its zone procedure does not explicitly state the response of every MCP when the containing zone is disabled. Older-edition wording is not merged into this baseline.
sourceGaps.impact: Z2, the zone used in disable/enable lessons, contains no MCP. Lessons use an optical sensor for individual disablement.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: Manufacturer clarification or a verified target-firmware test of MCP response under zone disablement.

sourceGaps.title: Verify, U buttons and external output relationships are commissioned
sourceGaps.detail: The operator guide describes configuration-dependent Verify and U-button functions; interface outputs can belong to sectors. The training fixture cannot infer a real site cause-and-effect matrix.
sourceGaps.impact: Help explains these functions, but the generic operator lessons do not assign universal U-button tasks or an invented verification period.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: Site configuration, labelled U-button functions and target firmware details.

sourceGaps.title: FARE key positions need additional confirmation
sourceGaps.detail: The operator FARE on/off description and the commissioning menu diagram do not provide one unambiguous shared physical-key sequence for all target variants.
sourceGaps.impact: FARE/FPE purpose is explained with source pages; no guessed FARE/FPE action route is included in the guided lessons.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A verified full-size EN panel menu recording and firmware identifier.

sourceGaps.title: A delay-description row is labelled Sounder in the operator table
sourceGaps.detail: The panel drawing identifies a Delay lamp, while page 9 repeats Sounder against the delay-block description. The source inconsistency is retained in the audit.
sourceGaps.impact: Help uses the physical panel layout and does not teach the duplicated table label as a separate second Sounder indicator.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: Manufacturer erratum or a confirmed panel photograph.

sourceGaps.title: Repair instructions conflict with other verified menu positions
sourceGaps.detail: The operator repair section assigns Test/Eng to F1 although the main-menu drawing and display-test procedure use F4. Other post-authentication positions also differ.
sourceGaps.impact: The operator lessons do not turn Repair into a clear-fault shortcut or simulate that unresolved engineering route.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: The target firmware engineering menu and the applicable manufacturer correction.

trainingNotes: All addresses, locations and scenarios are invented training data. Customer practice PIN 2468 and engineering practice PIN 3917 are fictional and are not manufacturer defaults or real-site credentials.
Hints identify a physical button for the learner to press; enabling hints must never operate the panel or change a simulated protection state.
Acknowledge steps ask the learner to inspect the panel; their button is part of the lesson UI, not an extra GENT key.
Set-input and set-fault actions are explicitly labelled trainer controls representing external conditions; they are not keypad commands.
The printer is fitted but switched off in the fixture, so the conditional Display/Print branch is skipped.

Timer-dependent completion uses elapsed simulation time. The display-test exercise keeps its existing timing. The full walk-test lesson pauses automatic test timing and uses an explicit Advance 5 seconds action; free-practice zone tests run automatically.
The module follows this documented panel generation and does not claim that every GENT firmware, site or panel family has identical menus.
The full walk-test lesson requires input restoration, an explicit Zone Test Off commit and final normal checks. An ended alarm cycle or a closed menu never substitutes for those outcomes.
